fixes.explanation: Shepherd is a lovely word, friend, but it's not the one in this verse. Moses says “…our dwelling place through all generations.” So the picture is a home, and it reaches through all generations. Keep the shepherd in your pocket, because this psalm is going to move in a different direction.

A day gone by. The psalm says a thousand years in His sight “…are but a day that passes, or a watch of the night.” A thousand years, and in His sight it's like a day passing. Meanwhile I get impatient when my first batch takes twelve minutes.

A lifetime is a long stretch, friend, but that's not the picture here. The psalm says a thousand years in His sight “…are but a day that passes, or a watch of the night.” So the likeness is a day that passes, not a lifetime. I think that's the point of the picture: time looks very different from where He stands.

That's the opposite direction, friend. The verse doesn't make a thousand years sound endless. A thousand years in His sight “…are but a day that passes, or a watch of the night.” It's a big span, set beside a day that passes.

Offerings aren't what this verse is about. It says, “You have set our iniquities before You, our secret sins in the light of Your presence.” It's a heavy line. The things we keep hidden are set in the light of His presence.

Seventy, or eighty if we're strong. That's how the verse puts it: “The length of our days is seventy years—or eighty if we are strong…” It's a short window, friend. The verse goes on to say the days quickly pass, and we fly away.
This one's true, friend. The verse says, “Your wrath matches the fear You are due.” It's a heavy line. Moses puts it right there in the psalm.

A heart of wisdom! The prayer says, “So teach us to number our days, that we may present a heart of wisdom.” He doesn't ask to number days just to count them. The reason he gives is wisdom. That's a better reason than the one I had back in the junk drawer, where I counted the dust as it fell.

Their children. The prayer says, “May Your work be shown to Your servants, and Your splendor to their children.” Moses is looking past his own generation. He asks that the next generation see God's splendor too.

City walls aren't in this verse. The prayer ends, “establish for us the work of our hands—yes, establish the work of our hands!” It's the work of their hands, and he says it twice. Everyday work, right there in the prayer.
